period_summary: Citations are heavily concentrated in the 2nd through 4th centuries CE, reflecting the passage's centrality to early Christological argument. This density reveals that Ps 110:1 was among the most actively deployed proof-texts in the church, generating both precise quotation and interpretive paraphrase across all major regions.

citations.cited_text: Εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου· Κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου, ἕως ἂν θῶ τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου.
citations.text_form_note: Justin's wording aligns closely with the LXX tradition (Rahlfs Ps 109:1), including 'ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου' and the 'ἕως ἂν θῶ' construction. He shows no dependence on a Hebraizing recension and does not reflect the MT's 'lě-ḏāwid' superscription debate.
citations.theological_use: Justin deploys the verse as his primary proof that the pre-existent Christ is a second divine LORD addressed by the Father, thus establishing the two-powers-in-heaven framework against Jewish interlocutors. The double use of κύριος is exegetically central to his Christology.
citations.transmission_implication: Justin's consistent LXX-aligned citation across multiple works suggests the pre-Hexaplaric LXX was already the settled scriptural form for Greek-speaking Christians in the mid-2nd century.

citations.cited_text: Dixit Dominus Domino meo: Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum.
citations.text_form_note: The Old Latin (Vetus Latina) rendering 'Dixit Dominus Domino meo' reproduces the double-κύριος construction of the LXX and the 'scabellum pedum tuorum' closely mirrors 'ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου.' The Demonstratio preserves an Armenian tradition ultimately traceable to the same LXX Vorlage.
citations.theological_use: Irenaeus uses the verse to refute Gnostic dualism, arguing that the Father directly addresses the Son and that Christ's lordship is grounded in the Old Testament revelation, not a secondary aeon.
citations.transmission_implication: Irenaeus's Latin and Armenian witnesses confirm that Vetus Latina translations were made from LXX exemplars already standardized by the late 2nd century, not from Hebrew.

citations.cited_text: Dixit Dominus ad Dominum meum: Sede ad dexteram meam, donec posuero inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum.
citations.text_form_note: Tertullian's 'ad dexteram meam' slightly varies from Irenaeus's 'a dextris meis' but both ultimately reflect LXX ἐκ δεξιῶν μου. His use of 'donec posuero' (subjunctive variant) may represent a distinct Vetus Latina manuscript tradition rather than a different Vorlage.
citations.theological_use: In Adversus Praxean Tertullian exploits the two 'Dominus' forms to argue for a real distinction of Father and Son as persons within one divine substance, making this verse foundational for his Trinitarian grammar.
citations.transmission_implication: Minor Latin variants between Irenaeus and Tertullian suggest the Vetus Latina for this psalm was not yet uniformly standardized, though all forms derive from a common LXX-based source.

citations.work: Selecta in Psalmos; Contra Celsum; De Principiis
citations.chapter_section: Sel. Ps. 109:1 (PG 12:1565); C. Cels. VI.78; De Princ. I.3.1
citations.cited_text: Εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου· Κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου, ἕως ἂν θῶ τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου.
citations.text_form_note: Origen cites the standard LXX text in most contexts but in his Hexapla he records Aquila's rendering (τῷ κυρίῳ μου — נְאֻם יְהוָה לַאדֹנִי) and Symmachus's variant, showing he was fully aware of the Hebrew tradition. His mixed classification reflects that he actively compared text forms in his scholarly work, even while pastorally using the LXX.
citations.theological_use: Origen uses the verse in De Principiis to argue for the eternal generation of the Son and his subordinate-yet-divine status, and in Contra Celsum to demonstrate that Jewish scriptures themselves prophesy Christ's enthronement.
citations.transmission_implication: Origen's Hexaplaric work on this verse is the earliest documented collation of Hebrew and multiple Greek versions, indicating that by the early 3rd century textual pluralism was recognized and systematically addressed.

citations.cited_text: Εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου· Κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου, ἕως ἂν θῶ τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου.
citations.text_form_note: Eusebius consistently cites the standard LXX wording and in his Commentary explicitly discusses the Hexaplaric variants, endorsing the LXX as the authoritative Christian text while noting Aquila's stricter Hebrew rendering. He preserves the LXX 'ἕως ἂν θῶ' against Aquila's more literal form.
citations.theological_use: Eusebius uses the verse as his premier proof of Christ's post-resurrection enthronement and divine Lordship, situating it within his broader demonstration that the Hebrew prophets testified to two divine figures.
citations.transmission_implication: Eusebius's extensive commentary preserves a wealth of recensional data, confirming that the LXX text of Ps 109:1 was stable in the Caesarean tradition while awareness of Hebrew-based recensions was growing.

citations.work: Orationes contra Arianos; Expositiones in Psalmos
citations.cited_text: Εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου· Κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου.
citations.text_form_note: Athanasius cites the LXX form without Hexaplaric asterisks or Aquila variants, suggesting he worked from a standard Alexandrian LXX manuscript unaffected by Origenic revisions in this verse. His omission of the second half in several contexts is a rhetorical truncation, not a textual variant.
citations.theological_use: Athanasius mobilizes the verse against Arian exegesis, arguing that 'Sit at my right hand' implies co-essential divine status and is not a reward granted to a created being, directly engaging Arian citations of the same text.
citations.transmission_implication: Athanasius's citations demonstrate that the anti-Arian controversy crystallized around specific wordings of this verse, making its LXX text form the doctrinally normative one in Egyptian Christianity.

citations.work: Expositio in Psalmum 109; Homiliae in Matthaeum
citations.cited_text: Εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου· Κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου, ἕως ἂν θῶ τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου.
citations.text_form_note: Chrysostom's citation matches the Rahlfs LXX text closely and he shows no engagement with the Hexaplaric apparatus, indicating he used a standard liturgical LXX text rather than a scholarly recension. The Antiochene school's characteristic literary use of the LXX is fully evident here.
citations.theological_use: Chrysostom uses the verse homiletically to stress Christ's victorious enthronement and the subjection of enemies as an eschatological promise, emphasizing the pastoral dimensions of Christological kingship for his congregation.
citations.transmission_implication: Chrysostom's uncritical use of the LXX at Antioch confirms that the standard, pre-Hexaplaric LXX text was the living liturgical text in the East Syrian tradition by the late 4th century.

citations.cited_text: Dixit Dominus Domino meo: Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum.
citations.text_form_note: Augustine cites the Old Latin (Vetus Latina) version which is a translation of the LXX. He notes in Enarrationes that 'Dixit Dominus Domino meo' reflects two distinct persons, a reading made possible by the LXX's double κύριος and impossible from the Hebrew where the second word is 'adoni' (אֲדֹנִי), not the divine name. He was aware of Jerome's new Latin translation but defends the Vetus Latina form pastorally.
citations.theological_use: Augustine uses the verse as a cornerstone of his Trinitarian theology in De Trinitate and as a pastoral Christological proof in Enarrationes, arguing that the double Dominus reveals the co-equality yet personal distinction of Father and Son.
citations.transmission_implication: Augustine's defense of the Vetus Latina against Jerome's Hebraica veritas signals the emerging tension between LXX-based Christian tradition and the MT-aligned Vulgate, a tension directly visible in this verse.

transmission_synthesis: The patristic citation evidence for Ps 110:1 (LXX 109:1) is strikingly uniform: across eight witnesses spanning the 2nd to 5th centuries and covering Rome, Carthage, Alexandria, Caesarea, Antioch, and the Latin West, every father either cites or presupposes the LXX text form, including the theologically decisive double κύριος/Dominus rendering. No father up to the 5th century cites a form closer to the MT's nĕʾum YHWH lĕʾādōnî, which would render 'The oracle of the LORD to my lord' and lacks the second divine title; this absence is itself significant, since the LXX's κύριος-for-אֲדֹנִי opened the Christological reading the entire tradition exploited. Origen alone demonstrates awareness of the Hebrew-aligned recensions (Aquila, Symmachus), but even he does not displace the LXX as his authoritative text. This collectively implies that the LXX form of Ps 109:1 was transmitted in early Christianity as a fixed, liturgically embedded text, insulated from Hebraizing revision until at least Jerome, whose Iuxta Hebraeos version introduced the MT tradition into Latin Christianity but met with resistance precisely here.
transmission_synthesis_plain: Early Christian writers from the 2nd to the 5th century, across every region and language, consistently quote this psalm verse in the Greek Septuagint form rather than in any Hebrew-based version. This uniformity tells us that the Greek translation had become the authoritative Scripture for Christians so thoroughly that even scholars like Origen and Augustine, who knew other versions existed, continued to use it. The verse's theological importance for proving Christ's divine status actually reinforced its textual stability, since changing the wording would have undermined the Christological argument built on it.

notable_variants.reading: Double κύριος / Dominus: 'Εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου' / 'Dixit Dominus Domino meo'
notable_variants.significance: The LXX's rendering of אֲדֹנִי (ʾādōnî, 'my lord') as κύριος created a second divine title absent in the Hebrew, enabling the entire patristic two-persons Christological reading. This single translation choice, unanimously adopted by the Fathers, drove the verse's doctrinal career and makes it a paradigm case of how the LXX's text form shaped Christian theology.

notable_variants.reading: ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου vs. Aquila's more literal rendering
notable_variants.significance: The LXX's 'footstool of your feet' is a somewhat interpretive expansion of the Hebrew הֲדֹם רַגְלֶיךָ; Aquila's recension tightened this, but no Father outside the Hexaplaric tradition adopted Aquila's form, demonstrating that Aquila's revisions did not penetrate the Christian liturgical-homiletical stream even when scholars knew of them.

notable_variants.reading: ἕως ἂν θῶ / donec ponam vs. ἕως θήσω (minor Greek MS variants)
notable_variants.significance: Slight Latin variation in the rendering of 'until' (donec posuero vs. donec ponam) reflects a bifurcation in Vetus Latina manuscript traditions rather than different Vorlagen, confirming that multiple Latin translations of the same Greek LXX base text were circulating simultaneously in North Africa.

bibcrit_assessment.title: LXX's Double Kyrios Locked Christian Psalm Text
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The most significant finding is the total absence of MT-aligned citation in eight widely distributed patristic witnesses: no Father, not even those with direct access to Hebrew scholarship, ever deployed the Hebrew text's ʾādōnî in a way that undermined the double-divine-name reading. This implies the verse's theological function actively stabilized its LXX text form against revisional pressure, a feedback loop between dogma and transmission visible nowhere more clearly than here. The verse thus exemplifies Hengel's thesis that the LXX became 'Christian Scripture' in a sense that superseded its status as a translation, generating a textual tradition whose stability derived from doctrinal investment rather than merely scribal habit.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: Early Christians used a Greek translation of this psalm that made both figures in the verse appear to be called 'Lord,' which perfectly supported their belief that the Father was speaking to the divine Son. This theological usefulness froze the Greek wording in place so thoroughly that even scholars who knew the original Hebrew continued to quote the Greek version, because changing it would have weakened their central argument about Jesus.

_validation.confidence_note: The overall textual argument is sound and well-established, but several specific citation references and attributions require verification and some claims overreach the evidence.

flagged_claims.reason: Irenaeus does cite Ps 110:1, but the specific reference to AH III.6.1 should be verified; the verse appears in multiple places in AH and the Demonstratio.

flagged_claims.claim: Tertullian, Adv. Marc. V.9; Adv. Prax. 11
flagged_claims.reason: Tertullian cites Ps 110:1 in Adv. Prax., but the specific chapter (11) and the Adv. Marc. V.9 reference need verification; Adv. Prax. 13 is a more commonly cited locus.

flagged_claims.claim: Origen, Sel. Ps. 109:1 (PG 12:1565); C. Cels. VI.78; De Princ. I.3.1
flagged_claims.reason: Specific PG column references and the De Principiis I.3.1 citation for Ps 110:1 are suspicious; the Selecta in Psalmos attribution to Origen is itself textually contested, and these precise loci require verification.

flagged_claims.claim: Athanasius, Or. Ar. II.14–15; Exp. Ps. 109
flagged_claims.reason: Athanasius does engage Ps 110:1 against Arians, but the precise Or. Ar. II.14-15 reference may be inaccurate; the more famous discussion is in Or. Ar. I and II at various points.
The PG column number and homily reference need verification; Chrysostom's commentary on Ps 109 LXX exists but precise loci should be checked.

flagged_claims.claim: Eusebius, Dem. Ev. IV.15; Comm. Ps. 109 (PG 23:1348–1360)
flagged_claims.reason: Specific column ranges in PG are easy to fabricate; should be verified against actual Migne edition.
Antioch is not typically classified as 'East Syrian' in scholarly usage; East Syrian refers to the Church of the East tradition (Persian), while Chrysostom represents Greek Antiochene tradition.
Irenaeus was bishop of Lyons (Gaul); listing as 'Other' is imprecise and his Latin transmission context matters for the Vetus Latina claims.

flagged_claims.claim: The Demonstratio preserves an Armenian tradition ultimately traceable to the same LXX Vorlage
flagged_claims.reason: The Armenian Demonstratio's Vorlage is debated; claiming direct LXX traceability for this specific verse is more confident than the evidence supports.

flagged_claims.claim: Origen's Hexaplaric work on this verse is the earliest documented collation of Hebrew and multiple Greek versions
flagged_claims.reason: True of the Hexapla generally, but framing it 'on this verse' as a distinctive milestone overstates what survives for Ps 110:1 specifically.

safe_claims: The LXX renders both terms with κύριος while the MT has YHWH and adoni
Justin Martyr cites Ps 110:1 multiple times in Dialogue with Trypho as a Christological proof
Augustine used the Vetus Latina and was aware of Jerome's Hebrew-based translation
Origen knew Aquila's and Symmachus's renderings via the Hexapla
The double κύριος/Dominus was central to Christological argument in the Fathers
Jerome's Iuxta Hebraeos translation introduced MT-aligned readings into Latin Christianity
Ps 110:1 was among the most frequently cited OT texts in early Christology
